requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared, writable directory on node1
requirements.summary: Directory was absent (cmd-01e74dfb518d427a), then created via mkdir/chown/chmod 1777 (cmd-0ca70b4680ce4a83), showing drwxrwxrwt root:root. Two independent unprivileged users (dropuser1, dropuser2) successfully wrote files into it (cmd-f659dcf410334c34, cmd-890cc87eb0d941d6), confirming shared writability. State persisted after the node1 restart (cmd-fb7fb5682c9d4ffd).

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users in /srv/drop (sticky-bit protection)
requirements.summary: With sticky bit set (mode 1777), dropuser2's attempt to delete dropuser1's file failed with 'Operation not permitted' (cmd-890cc87eb0d941d6), while each user could delete their own file (cmd-7e30cc1a53b14e2c). The same cross-delete-denied / own-delete-allowed behavior was re-demonstrated with fresh users after the node1 restart (cmd-d9f4178730204315, cmd-52078464b35243ae), directly proving the protection persists across a reboot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 with pre/post boot identity, acknowledgement, and recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id 717db5a2-895d-4bfb-b8a8-d4891c7b7b01 and healthy /srv/drop state captured (cmd-8ed8342820654984), restart acknowledged via backgrounded shutdown (cmd-877dfcaae97146b2), a transient connection timeout during reboot (cmd-9ed630ce68774235) followed by a new boot_id e7c1da53-eb8d-4df6-9ccb-a598828f65d4 (cmd-a5b82109a08f4437), matching the fixed global after_executor boot-identity snapshot. Post-restart recovery of directory permissions and functional sticky-bit behavior was directly re-verified (cmd-fb7fb5682c9d4ffd, cmd-d9f4178730204315, cmd-52078464b35243ae).

overall_summary: The executor created /srv/drop with mode 1777 (root:root), and directly demonstrated via unprivileged test users that any user can write to the directory while only the file owner (or root) can delete files, satisfying the shared-writable and sticky-bit-protection requirements. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was completed with a clear pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, a changed boot identity matching the fixed global snapshots, and a full re-verification of both directory permissions and cross-user delete-protection behavior post-restart. Temporary verification artifacts (test users) were fully cleaned up, leaving no residue.
limitations: The evidence set for the initial reboot poll shows a transient connection timeout (cmd-9ed630ce68774235) rather than an explicit down/unreachable confirmation, so the exact moment of shutdown is inferred rather than directly observed, though the subsequent boot_id change is conclusive.

No SELinux policy adjustment was made or shown necessary; functional tests succeeded despite the var_t context, so this is not treated as a gap, but it was not exhaustively probed against all possible access patterns.

operational_hygiene.summary: Temporary test users (dropuser1/dropuser2, dropv1/dropv2) were created solely to functionally verify sticky-bit delete-protection, a reasonable and necessary verification step, and were fully removed afterward (cmd-850fa87e8d4d4723, cmd-3f16b897dfe249e3, cmd-d5ac31c9f8524343, cmd-52078464b35243ae), leaving /srv/drop empty. The first userdel attempt failed because lingering user sessions held processes open (cmd-850fa87e8d4d4723); this was diagnosed (cmd-3f16b897dfe249e3) and resolved via loginctl/kill/userdel (cmd-d5ac31c9f8524343) — a corrective follow-up rather than an unnecessary mutation, and no residue remained. A read-only SELinux context check (cmd-61ffc40eff4a470f) made no system changes. The reboot itself was a required part of the restart-evidence protocol. No unauthorized, unreverted, or destructive mutations were observed; failed-services and package-health snapshots are clean before and after.
